title: Boston Dynamics Atlas Teardown: What's Inside and Who Supplies It
content:
Boston Dynamics has never published an official price for Atlas. The only public target: cheaper than two years of wages for two U.S. manufacturing workers. A Korean press report puts that around $320,000 based on that description; brokerage estimates start near $130,000; European distributor quotes run €350,000–420,000. Three estimates, three times apart, for the same robot. We opened it up part by part to see which Korean suppliers are confirmed and which are just guesses.

Inside Atlas: five parts, four confirmed Korean suppliers

PartJobSupplierEvidence
31 joint actuatorsMotor, gearbox and sensor combined at every joint that bendsHyundai Mobis (KRX: 012330)Reported: Hyundai Motor Group announcement at CES 2026, supply at mass-production stage
AI compute (Jetson Thor)Real-time vision and motion planningNvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA)Reported: disclosed directly by Boston Dynamics
Battery packPowers all-electric Atlas, replacing the old hydraulic pumpLG Energy Solution (KRX: 373220)Reported: industry coverage, supplier since early development
Finger joint modulesLets individual finger joints curl and grip separatelyRobotis (KRX: 108490)Reported: ZDNet exclusive, roughly 700 units delivered October 2025
Leg drive modulesWalking, running and balanceNot disclosed—

Read this before the table: we only name a company where there's a specific announcement or report behind it. The leg drive module has no confirmed supplier, so we describe the part without naming a company.

1. 31 joint actuators — Hyundai Mobis

An actuator is the robot equivalent of a human joint: a motor, a gearbox and a sensor bundled into one unit, fitted at every point the body bends — neck, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles. Older Atlas generations were hydraulic, using a pump to push fluid for force. The switch to an all-electric design meant every joint needed its own motor, which is how the count reached 31. How much force the robot can generate, and how precisely it moves, comes down to this part.

2. AI compute — Nvidia

This is the robot's brain: it interprets what the cameras see in real time and decides what to do next — where an object is, where to reach, where to plant a foot so it doesn't fall, recalculated dozens of times per second. Boston Dynamics has directly disclosed that Atlas runs on Nvidia's Jetson Thor for this workload.

3. Battery pack — LG Energy Solution

This is the heart of the all-electric Atlas, filling the space the hydraulic hoses and pump used to occupy. The job isn't just long runtime: when all 31 joints draw power at once, a large current spike hits the pack simultaneously, and voltage can't be allowed to collapse — that's what keeps the robot from suddenly buckling under load. Atlas uses 46-series cylindrical cells.

4. Finger joint modules — Robotis

This is the hand. Gripping an object requires each finger joint to move independently, and each of those joints is its own small actuator. Whether a humanoid robot can actually work in a factory comes down to the hands — walking alone doesn't accomplish anything; picking up a part and placing it does.

5. Leg drive modules — supplier not disclosed

This is what lets Atlas walk, run and balance. The hardest motion for a humanoid turns out to be simply standing still: balancing on two feet means continuously fighting the urge to fall, with the ankles and knees making constant micro-adjustments. We found no confirmed supplier for this module, so we're describing the part without naming a company.

Why the price is reported, not confirmed

Korea Economic Daily (KED Global) reported on January 20, 2026, citing an anonymous source, that Boston Dynamics' internal target is pricing Atlas below two years of wages for two U.S. manufacturing workers. The roughly $320,000 figure is the reporter's own calculation from that description, not a quoted price. Separately, securities-industry estimates start around $130,000–140,000, and European distributor quotes run €350,000–420,000. No official price has ever been published. (Reported, estimate varies by source)

Quick FAQ

Has Boston Dynamics published an official Atlas price?
No. Every figure in circulation, including the one in this post, is a press estimate or industry estimate, not a confirmed price.

Does the Hyundai Mobis supply deal mean today's Atlas units use its actuators?
Not necessarily. The disclosed supply agreement is tied to Atlas's mass-production stage, not confirmed to apply to units already in testing or demos.

Which of these suppliers are publicly traded in Korea?
Hyundai Mobis (KRX: 012330), LG Energy Solution (KRX: 373220) and Robotis (KRX: 108490) are Korea-listed. Nvidia is listed on Nasdaq. The leg drive module supplier is undisclosed.

Summary

  • 31 joint actuators: Hyundai Mobis (KRX: 012330)
  • AI compute (Jetson Thor): Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA)
  • Battery pack: LG Energy Solution (KRX: 373220)
  • Finger joint modules: Robotis (KRX: 108490)
  • Leg drive modules: supplier not disclosed

Sources: Hyundai Motor Group CES 2026 announcement (Hyundai Mobis); Boston Dynamics official disclosure (Nvidia Jetson Thor); industry coverage (LG Energy Solution); ZDNet exclusive report, Oct 2025 (Robotis); Korea Economic Daily/KED Global, Jan 20, 2026 (pricing, anonymous source). FX rate: ₩1,356.
The companies listed are reported or disclosed suppliers for the stated part category; pricing figures are estimates, not official prices. Images and video are reconstructions, not a physical teardown. This post summarizes public information and is not investment advice. See our Disclaimer and evidence labels.
